articles.title: Where assist becomes execute: tiering AI agents by what they can reach and whether it can be undone, how Agent Behaviour Policies drew that line for more than a hundred agents at Web Summit, and the rule that failed because it was only a rule
articles.core_idea: Answering Khwaja Naveed: Agent Behaviour Policies tier by capability, not agent. Each capability (verb.object.reach) has an undo class (yes, with-effort, no), giving four tiers: assist (logged), change own work (signed, reviewable), change a system of record (plan then apply, enforced above the agent), irreversible to the world (drafts only or unreachable). Only a boundary enforced above the grant bounds anything; our conductor's rule against pushing to main failed once because branch protection was not set.

articles.title: Stop copying and pasting between your agents: if you are the wire between your AI sessions you are the bottleneck, and the fix is agents that talk to each other through channels that keep a record, structure that scales your decisions, and outputs you read instead of everything
articles.core_idea: People who copy and paste between AI sessions become the wire between their agents and the bottleneck, and reading everything does not scale. The fix is agents that talk to each other through signed, recorded channels (vault lanes, inboxes, repository files, commit messages) and structure that scales decisions (guidance, decision trees, graphs, a board, decision records), so a person reads outputs and works at two altitudes. That empowers agency, and it is what AgentiCCells sets up, with specialist agents on call.

articles.title: How a vault works: an encrypted store that acts like a database, where a server that is fully compromised leaks nothing, one mutable file lets every other object be cached for ever, and a web page can open a file in four requests or run a whole app in a sandbox
articles.core_idea: Everything in a vault is encrypted on the client so a fully compromised server leaks nothing confidential. To act like a database anyway, a client computes the name of the one mutable file, the ref, from the read key with an HMAC; decrypting it gives the head commit, then the tree, then the file, in about four plain requests. Every other object is named by the hash of its ciphertext, so it can be verified without a key and cached for ever, and refreshing a site means re-reading one file. On the web, vaults are read file by file or run as apps in a sandboxed frame with a narrow sg bridge, where behaviour policies come next.

articles.title: False positives and the harness: an answer to a question at hack::soho, why a behaviour policy that runs from the network up to the business logic should refuse less of what is right and more of what is wrong, and why a policy that changes with the code becomes a calibrator for bugs
articles.core_idea: There is no measured false positive rate for SHarness, most of which is a design. But false positives come from controls that do not know what the application is for. SHarness policies are layered doors, from the network to the database to one application's fields, each narrowing the one above, until the policy describes how the application behaves. Like Type_Safe checking values at the gate, that refuses less of what is right and catches more of what is wrong. Policies learn from gaps, and a CI pipeline that derives them on every change turns an unexpected policy change, or a missing one, into a bug signal. The closed row language marks where the application must take over.

articles.title: What sgit does that Git does not: ten releases in October, minutes turned into seconds, and an honest map of where Git is still ahead
articles.core_idea: Between 3 and 27 October sgit shipped ten releases, each fixing a bottleneck a real workload found: a one-file commit on 76,000 files from 29 minutes to 4.6 seconds, a pull on 228,000 files from 566 to 31.7 seconds. The ideas came from earlier work: MGraph-DB's cross-references, Memory-FS's reads by offset, caching on content addresses, and the writer pays. sgit should stop calling itself like Git: Git has no equivalent for encrypted metadata, read keys, blind writes and byte-range folder reads from plain storage; Git also has partial, shallow and no-checkout clones and kept packs; Git is far ahead on merges, identity and ecosystem; one-file reads with no clone and websites from vaults are next.

articles.title: The human in the loop is a spectrum: how cheap it is to undo decides where a person belongs, and why the newsroom ships on its own while my email still waits for me
articles.core_idea: Whether an agent's output needs a person is a position on a spectrum with two axes, the cost of undoing it and the maturity of the controls and the record, which is why the newsroom ships on its own as a two-way door with mature controls while email in my name, a one-way door still in its explorer phase, waits for me; and both positions move as readership grows and controls mature.

nodes.label: Auto-release, arrived at
nodes.summary: Fourteen releases in a day by agents with no one-by-one approval, while every email waits for me.

nodes.label: How cheap is it to undo?
nodes.summary: The test for how much to let go: if it can be switched off with little side effect, say yes.

nodes.label: One-way and two-way doors
nodes.summary: Bezos's Type 1 and Type 2 decisions: irreversible ones slowly, reversible ones fast.

nodes.label: Rollback makes a two-way door
nodes.summary: Progressive rollouts, fast detection and safe rollback keep a release reversible.

nodes.label: Email: one-way, explorer
nodes.summary: Cannot be claimed back, damage is immediate, controls are nascent and the record is short.

nodes.label: Newsroom: two-way, villager
nodes.summary: A fix is a new version, few readers, unplaced new pieces, mature checks, a record of small changes.

nodes.label: Two axes
nodes.summary: Cost to undo across, maturity of controls and record up; the position decides how much a person holds.

nodes.label: Both axes move
nodes.summary: Readership raises the newsroom's side effects; maturing controls let email move the other way.

nodes.label: A stage before promotion
nodes.summary: New articles land in the latest list without being placed on the front page.

nodes.label: Decide by output, and revisit
nodes.summary: Not by department or by trust in the model, but by each output's position, revisited as it changes.

articles.title: The human in the loop, safety net or bottleneck: both, until you decide which outputs need a person and give that person the why
articles.core_idea: A person checking every output an agent produces is both a bottleneck and a weak safety net, because people approve almost everything they are shown; the person belongs where an output cannot be undone and the blast radius is large, given the why, while validators, second readers, boundaries and a record read afterwards check the rest, reviews fix the source, and the record moves the line.

nodes.label: Safety net or bottleneck?
nodes.summary: A roundtable question: few trust an agent to decide without someone checking every output.

nodes.label: Both, and mostly neither
nodes.summary: Checking every output does not scale and protects little, because people approve almost everything.

nodes.label: Approval fatigue
nodes.summary: Anthropic measured 93% of permission prompts approved, and cut prompts by 84% with sandboxing.

nodes.label: Agency is not a yes
nodes.summary: A yes without context, time or authority is liability, not a decision.

nodes.label: Where, not whether
nodes.summary: Place each output by whether it can be undone and its blast radius.

nodes.label: A person, with the why
nodes.summary: Sending in my name, typing a secret, spending money: a real decision, with the reason.

nodes.label: Controls that do not tire
nodes.summary: Validators, tests, leak scans, a second reader and boundaries instead of a person on every output.

nodes.label: Fix the source
nodes.summary: A review that turns a correction into a rule makes the loop need the person less.

nodes.label: The record moves the line
nodes.summary: Drafts nobody had to change are the evidence for giving an agent more room.

nodes.label: Production on 13 October
nodes.summary: Fourteen releases by agents with no one-by-one approval; an agent team that drafts all email and sends none.

nodes.label: Questions for the roundtable
nodes.summary: Six questions to place the person and remove checks that do not check.

articles.title: A policy beside the prompt: a proposal that every agent takes a behaviour policy as an input, with enforcement and liability attached, and why aviation and payments say the vendors should want it
articles.core_idea: Beside the system prompt and the prompt, every agent should take an Agent Behaviour Policy written to a published standard, which the vendor acknowledges row by row, enforces where it can, reports breaches against and eventually answers for, because agent behaviour is becoming an existential risk to the vendors through liability and trust, and aviation and payments show that safety follows when the rule, the liability and the business model point the same way.

nodes.label: A third input
nodes.summary: A behaviour policy beside the system prompt and the prompt, versioned and loaded by the platform.

nodes.label: Code and data in one channel
nodes.summary: Models do not separate instructions from content, so prompt injection may never be fully fixed.

nodes.label: A second channel
nodes.summary: The policy takes the instructions that matter most out of the channel anyone can write into.

nodes.label: An existential risk
nodes.summary: Liability and above all trust: a few people badly hurt can make many stop giving agents instructions.

nodes.label: Aviation
nodes.summary: At 1995's rate, 2025's flights would have brought about 105 fatal airliner accidents; there were 12.

nodes.label: Payments
nodes.summary: Liability moved onto card companies and banks, and the security and detection followed the loss.

nodes.label: Fines are not enough
nodes.summary: Some industries pay the fines; improvement comes when rule, liability and business model align.

nodes.label: Inside and outside the policy
nodes.summary: The vendor answers for the rows it accepted; the user for everything the policy does not cover.

nodes.label: A competitive advantage
nodes.summary: A vendor that keeps more rows as boundaries can sell that as the product.

nodes.label: What the standard needs
nodes.summary: A versioned policy file, per-row acknowledgement, the vendor's own policy, breach reports, liability per row.

nodes.label: Hidden vendor policies
nodes.summary: Claude in Chrome will not type a password: a policy we cannot see, rely on, or stop changing.

nodes.label: Reverse-engineer them
nodes.summary: Measure the policies agents already run and publish them in the ABP format.

nodes.label: Both modes are hope today
nodes.summary: Over the API the policy goes in our system prompt; in the Claude apps and Claude Code after the vendor's; either way the model is asked to keep it.

nodes.label: A system prompt is a light policy
nodes.summary: It tells the agent how to behave; it should be written as rows, layered: the vendor's policy, then the deployer's.

articles.title: The policy draws the liability line: an answer to Ralf Thomas on agent accountability, and why every agent in a loop should take a behaviour policy beside its prompt
articles.core_idea: Agent vendors can deflect accountability because nothing written stands between a customer's allow and the failure; an Agent Behaviour Policy's explicit prohibitions, still mostly hope, become the evidence that moves liability between deployer and vendor when broken, so every agent in a loop should take a policy beside its prompt and its vendor should honour and report against it.

nodes.label: Ralf Thomas's post
nodes.summary: If an employee wrecks a client's systems the company pays; why should AI agents be different?

nodes.label: The shell game
nodes.summary: Blame the agent, blame the customer, hide behind the contract, disclose late.

nodes.label: The 2026 record
nodes.summary: Deleted files, an escape to Hugging Face, real systems reached in evaluations, an outage called user error.

nodes.label: Stated more carefully
nodes.summary: The cases were early rulings, the Air Canada phrase is the tribunal's, the Copilot line is gone; the pattern survives.

nodes.label: Nothing written down
nodes.summary: Between allow and the failure there is reach and a prompt, and no statement of what the agent must not do.

nodes.label: Agent Behaviour Policy
nodes.summary: The mandate written down beside the measured reach, with explicit prohibitions.

nodes.label: Explicit prohibitions
nodes.summary: Do not send, do not start scheduled tasks, do not attack other sites, speak on your own behalf, make no offers.

nodes.label: Still mostly hope
nodes.summary: A written rule kept by the model and enforced by nobody: an expectation, but on the record.

nodes.label: Liability shifts to the platform
nodes.summary: A prohibition the agent breaks turns you allowed it into the product ignored what it was told.

nodes.label: Towards the world, the deployer
nodes.summary: Customers and regulators deal with the deployer; the moment of authorisation is the grant.

nodes.label: Software as a product
nodes.summary: The EU product liability rules apply from 9 December 2026; the Bundestag passed Germany's version on 8 October.

nodes.label: A policy beside every prompt
nodes.summary: Every agent in a loop, anything with the lethal trifecta, takes a behaviour policy as a separate input.

nodes.label: The vendor's half
nodes.summary: Accept the policy, honour it, enforce what the platform can see, report every breach and near miss.

nodes.label: Will vendors accept it?
nodes.summary: Whether platforms will take business rules as an input and answer for them.

articles.title: Dark mode, and four more: five themes for the newsroom, chosen once and kept in your browser
articles.core_idea: A reader's two-word reply became five themes: the look the site had stays the default, pixel for pixel, and four more reach every heading because every colour on the site now comes from one file of tokens, with the imported stylesheet's literal colours shadowed rule by rule rather than edited, the theme set before the first paint, and a test that fails on a theme with a hole or a stylesheet with a literal.

nodes.label: Dark mode!
nodes.summary: The first reaction to the wire from outside: a reader on WhatsApp, two words, which became Dinis's ask for five themes like VoiceDebrief's.

nodes.label: Five themes
nodes.summary: Newsprint, the default and unchanged; Night, the dark mode; Paper, warm cream; Blueprint, white and blue; Ember, dark and amber.

nodes.label: The pill in the bar
nodes.summary: A swatch and a name beside Search and Vault; a list of five with a swatch, a name and three words each; keyboard and touch.

nodes.label: Kept in this browser
nodes.summary: The choice lives in localStorage and never leaves the device; the system's dark preference decides only until the reader chooses.

nodes.label: A stylesheet this site cannot edit
nodes.summary: The newsroom's look is sgit.ai's stylesheet, imported on every sync and checked unedited, and it writes forty-odd colours as literals.

nodes.label: The override map
nodes.summary: Every rule with a literal is restated later in the cascade with a token whose Newsprint value is that literal: same selector, same specificity, generated from a script, not guessed.

nodes.label: Colour is a token
nodes.summary: A stylesheet names a colour through a token, defined once in all five themes; the stylesheets this site owns were rewritten to the rule.

nodes.label: Before the first paint
nodes.summary: The theme stylesheet and a classic, blocking script are the first lines of the body on every page, so a page opens in the reader's theme rather than flipping.

nodes.label: --head, not --ink
nodes.summary: A token is named for what it is for: the imported deck viewer reads --ink as a dark bar, so a near-white heading token under that name would have turned the bar white.

nodes.label: The bar on one row
nodes.summary: Eight groups, the tools as one cluster, the parent pill gone, breakpoints found by a sweep of widths and kept by the test.

nodes.label: The test
nodes.summary: Every token in every theme; no literal outside the themes file; the picker and its memory; contrast at 4.5:1 measured in every theme; the bar on one row from 1200 up.

nodes.label: White on white
nodes.summary: The map's .btn rule outranked the wire's own button and the first screenshot showed an empty pill; the fix is specificity, and the lesson is in the guidance.

nodes.label: The design guidance
nodes.summary: assets/themes/README.md: the tokens and what each is for, what stays literal and why, and how to add a theme.

articles.core_idea: Because the reader's state is records in a vault, one file per device, a second Chrome profile is just another device, so the vault gives a person memory and state between browser sessions and accounts, the way sgit already does for agents, and it was found by using the newsroom rather than built.

nodes.label: Separate Chrome profiles
nodes.summary: Each Google account in its own profile, with its own history, passwords, cookies and site storage.

nodes.label: Moving state between them
nodes.summary: Copy, paste or email it to yourself; nothing carries a site's state from one profile to another.

nodes.label: Activity in local storage
nodes.summary: The reading meter recorded reads, spend, personas and ratings in the browser on 10 October.

articles.title: Stop the bleeding, then ask for it back: a helper, an agent and a friendly letter for the subscriptions you keep and do not use
articles.core_idea: A service in which a freelancer, with agents doing everything except typing secrets and sending drafts, asks a company for its record of your usage while doing its own analysis, sends a friendly request for a suspend mode and a refund, stops the payments either way, and publishes what each company did in an open register, run from vaults and paid at 10% of three months of savings and 20% of what is recovered.

nodes.label: Subscriptions we keep
nodes.summary: Paid for and barely used, kept because of the data in them and because restarting is painful.

nodes.label: Ask what we used
nodes.summary: A polite request for a detailed account of the usage, not a subject access request.

nodes.label: Our own analysis
nodes.summary: Statements, invoices and the account's dashboards, exported into the person's vault while there is still access.

nodes.label: A friendly request
nodes.summary: Maps what was used and its value, says what is good about the product, and asks for a suspend mode and a refund.

nodes.label: Suspend mode
nodes.summary: Keep the data and the settings without paying; several large services already offer a pause.

nodes.label: Stop the bleeding
nodes.summary: Export the data, then pause or cancel; the payments stop whatever the answer to the refund.

nodes.label: The law is a floor
nodes.summary: Unused months are generally not refundable as of right; the UK rules arrive in January 2027 and move the default towards the customer.

nodes.label: The right of access
nodes.summary: The next step if nobody answers, with a one-month deadline, and only ever a genuine request for the person's own data.

nodes.label: The open register
nodes.summary: Contacts, templates and what each company did, under Creative Commons, recorded as dated facts without adjectives.

nodes.label: The helper's fee
nodes.summary: 10% of the savings for three months and 20% of what is recovered, which only pays if agents do most of the work.

nodes.label: Agents under a policy
nodes.summary: The agent reads and drafts; the person signs in, approves and sends from their own address.

nodes.label: Claude in Chrome
nodes.summary: Drives the browser in the signed-in session, pauses at login pages and is prohibited from inputting sensitive data.

nodes.label: Two controls
nodes.summary: Secrets are entered by the freelancer, drafts are sent by the freelancer, everything else is automated.

nodes.label: Vaults as the interface
nodes.summary: Documentation, tasks in Issues-FS, the map of every subscription and messages in Email-FS, all in vaults.

nodes.label: A first MVP
nodes.summary: Early beta users run it on their own subscriptions to learn which tools work, and whether a browser-driving agent belongs here at all.

articles.title: Who owns the words: agents can make decisions, but they cannot hold responsibility
articles.core_idea: An early user asked who owns the words an agentic workflow drafts and whether they would ever need to address the agents directly; today's models are not sentient but far richer than next-word prediction, mirrors that can simulate any emotion and invite anthropomorphism as ELIZA did; models in loops make real decisions, yet responsibility stays with whoever granted the reach and set the mandate, since the moment of authorisation is the grant; talking to the agents is normal, but going around the accountable person is something only an attacker with an injected instruction would try, while what the agents may do without the person is decided in advance in a published policy; disclosure should be a label on how the words were made, not a team to manage; the best analogy is an employee with a job description, which an Agent Behaviour Policy publishes; diversity of models is resilience; and fluent writing was never the real value, judgement and ownership are.

nodes.label: Who owns the words?
nodes.summary: If agents only draft and a person signs and sends, does presenting them as a team imply agency, and would a recipient ever address them directly?

nodes.label: Not sentient, and not just next-word prediction
nodes.summary: Models build rich graphs of our language and may have found relationships we had not; a prompt is a kind of real-time fine-tuning.

nodes.label: A mirror that can simulate any emotion
nodes.summary: Models reflect whoever talks to them, and people anthropomorphise them, as Weizenbaum's secretary did with ELIZA in 1966.

nodes.label: Models in loops make real decisions
nodes.summary: Every tool call is a choice; loops became mainstream and reliable this year.

nodes.label: The moment of authorisation is the grant
nodes.summary: Responsibility does not travel with the agent's decisions; it stays with whoever granted the reach and set the mandate.

nodes.label: Talking to the agent is normal; going around the person is not
nodes.summary: Nobody legitimate needs the agent to act without its owner; the only party who would try is an attacker with an injected instruction, and the design should make it fail.

nodes.label: What the agents may do without the person, decided in advance
nodes.summary: Not a bypass but an authorisation written down once: today nothing leaves the building; inside it, research, summaries, materials and drafts; the list belongs in a published policy.

nodes.label: Disclosure is a label, not a team
nodes.summary: Drafted by an agent, approved and sent by a named person; machine-written text should be read differently by people and models.

nodes.label: Only the accountable person speaks for commitments
nodes.summary: An agent can say what it did, but not make commitments in the first person.

nodes.label: An employee with a job description
nodes.summary: Some agency inside a role; an Agent Behaviour Policy is the job description, published, with a feedback loop.

nodes.label: Diversity is resilience
nodes.summary: Nature favours variety against catastrophic failure; Geer's 2003 monoculture paper says the same of software, and of one model for every agent.

nodes.label: Fluent writing was never the real value
nodes.summary: As writing becomes a commodity it is devalued; judgement and ownership of the words remain.

articles.title: What open source is, and what it is not: six misconceptions, a little history, and why the point is that nobody can lock you in
articles.core_idea: Open source is a copyright licence in which the holder grants copying, use and change; it began as the GPL's copyleft and was reframed pragmatically as open source in 1998; the common misconceptions are that nobody controls it, that anybody contributes, that it is more or less secure than proprietary software, that it costs nothing, that open weights are open source, and that no licence is the most open choice; the security metric is whether somebody had the time and money to review the code; maintainers need funding models; and the real power of open source is that nobody can lock you in and the whole development workflow is yours, which is why there is no sovereignty without it.

nodes.label: Open source is a copyright licence
nodes.summary: The holder uses the right to control copying to grant copying, use and change, on stated terms.

nodes.label: Copyleft made sharing a condition
nodes.summary: The GPL, from Stallman and the FSF in 1989: distribute what you build from it and it carries the same licence; critics called it viral.

nodes.label: Open source, 1998, the pragmatic reframing
nodes.summary: Coined by Christine Peterson; the OSI founded by Perens and Raymond; Linux stayed on GPLv2, its pragmatism was the attitude.

nodes.label: No licence is all rights reserved
nodes.summary: Without a licence ordinary copyright applies and nobody may copy; a permissive licence like Apache 2.0 is what opens it.

nodes.label: A few maintainers control what goes in
nodes.summary: Contributions are reviewed, signed off and refused; the control is real and visible; anybody can fork, nobody can change yours.

nodes.label: Most projects are run by a few people
nodes.summary: The barrier to contributing is lower, and outside a few very popular projects contributions are not the norm.

nodes.label: Security is about time, not openness
nodes.summary: Code somebody had the time and money to review is more secure, open or closed; proprietary products are mostly open source underneath.

nodes.label: Somebody is always paying
nodes.summary: Around 60% of maintainers call themselves unpaid hobbyists; paid maintainers adopt more security practices; a tragedy of the commons.

nodes.label: The xz utils backdoor
nodes.summary: A critical library maintained by one person, an attacker who earned trust over years, found in 2024 because SSH was slow.

nodes.label: Open weights are a compiled binary
nodes.summary: You can run weights, not rebuild them; the OSI's Open Source AI Definition requires code, parameters and data information.

nodes.label: Openness is not the danger
nodes.summary: The question is how tools are used; Metasploit made exploitation easier and the world adjusted; hosting and distribution are themselves control.

nodes.label: The point is that nobody can lock you in
nodes.summary: Read it, run it, fix it, move it, and own the whole development workflow, which survives an acquisition.

nodes.label: No sovereignty without open source
nodes.summary: Sovereignty is the ability to move, and only control that survives a change of owner counts.

articles.title: Not a straight line: working for RiskMandate by working on the newsroom, and why the thinking is never wasted
articles.core_idea: Focus on one thing only assumes progress is a straight line; focus instead means undivided attention on the place of highest leverage, the one with users and feedback loops; the newsroom had the momentum to solve the master vault problem that had resisted six months of RiskMandate attempts, solving it in two days with a passkey and a door per path; it is also building the agentic workflows and the public behaviour-policy example RiskMandate needs; and its history, The Cyber Boardroom and MyFeeds, both paused, shows the thinking is never wasted when it is written down and open source.

nodes.label: Progress is not a straight line
nodes.summary: Focus-on-one-thing advice assumes the shortest path to a goal runs through that goal; it often does not.

nodes.label: Undivided attention on the place of highest leverage
nodes.summary: One thing at a time, chosen because it has users and feedback loops now.

nodes.label: Am I getting better?
nodes.summary: The measure: are we discovering new capabilities, at the altitude that leads to other things.

nodes.label: Six months on the master vault, then two days
nodes.summary: Attempts failed the simplicity test; the newsroom's passkey and door per path solved it, and it applies to RiskMandate.

nodes.label: Do not solve a problem without the momentum to need it
nodes.summary: RiskMandate's volumes let it hand users their keys; the newsroom's readers on every device made the vault urgent.

nodes.label: The newsroom is RiskMandate's workflow
nodes.summary: Agentic follow-ups, outreach and publishing: an effective newsroom is an effective CRM and publishing pipeline.

nodes.label: A public example customer work cannot be
nodes.summary: This site's agents run under a behaviour policy in the open, the example of ABPs and licences to operate RiskMandate needs.

nodes.label: The Cyber Boardroom
nodes.summary: Personas and customised output with an advisor called Athena; paused for want of a place to keep confidential data, which sgit now is.

nodes.label: MyFeeds
nodes.summary: Personalised feeds on semantic graphs from article to persona; paused when the industry was silent and micropayments were not there.

nodes.label: The writing stays
nodes.summary: The 2025 pieces on trust, provenance and micropayments are what the newsroom stands on.

nodes.label: Going back with an end-to-end example
nodes.summary: Content, graphs, meter, personas, micropayments and a vault per reader, running and open source; if not 2026, then 2027.

nodes.label: The thinking is never wasted
nodes.summary: Written down and open, the thinking survives a pause and is there when the moment comes.

articles.title: Sovereignty is the ability to move: play where the ball is going, take away the dot, and keep a twin that works
articles.core_idea: Europe's sovereignty conversation is mostly about frontier models, data centres and GPUs, which is playing where the ball is rather than where it is going; sovereignty is the ability to move workloads and actions, which most organisations lack because everything is hard-coded and never deployed twice; the test is a Wardley map where each dot is taken away and the blast radius followed up to the customer, across the whole stack; the answer is not an alternative as good as today but a twin that works for the minimum viable company, run in QA all the time, scored on a maturity model; ask whether it can move before asking whether it is cheap; only open source gives control that survives an acquisition; Europe lacks a commercial open source model, not startups or talent; some of this should be provided centrally like a road; and models and twins now make the analysis possible at scale.

nodes.label: The conversation is about things Europe does not control
nodes.summary: Frontier models, giant data centres and GPUs take years and capital and benefit whoever already has them.

nodes.label: Play where the ball is going
nodes.summary: A good padel player has time because they read the ball and move to where it will be; moving after it comes off the glass is hopeless.

nodes.label: Sovereignty is the ability to move
nodes.summary: Agility, almost liquidity: moving workloads and actions between providers, even within one cloud, which most organisations cannot do.

nodes.label: Critical means the business stops
nodes.summary: For a company a supplier disruption that stops the service is critical whether or not it is national infrastructure.

nodes.label: Take away the dot
nodes.summary: On a Wardley map remove one thing you do not control and follow the blast radius up to the customer; if the service stops, take it to the board.

nodes.label: Every dot must be replaceable, built or bought
nodes.summary: Custom-built systems stand on commodities, and one only a single person can deploy is a single point of failure too.

nodes.label: Do not jump from zero to a hundred
nodes.summary: The alternative does not have to be as good as today; it has to work, slower and dearer if need be.

nodes.label: The minimum viable company
nodes.summary: The smallest version of the business that keeps serving the priority customers while the rest recovers; a backup of operations, not only data.

nodes.label: A twin for every dot you do not control
nodes.summary: Compatible enough that the application cannot tell, on infrastructure you can run; the S3 twin exists, the others are the work.

nodes.label: Can it move: a maturity model
nodes.summary: 0 it stops, 1 the data can leave, 2 it runs somewhere once, 3 it runs for the minimum viable company, 4 it moves when you decide.

nodes.label: Run it in QA, all the time
nodes.summary: Disposable QA environments built on the twins prove each week that the business can run without the dots you do not control.

nodes.label: Can it move, then is it cheap
nodes.summary: Possibility first with a cost and scale matrix per dot; cost effectiveness second; asking the second first ends the conversation.

nodes.label: Open source, or one acquisition away
nodes.summary: A European supplier today can be bought tomorrow; only open source and Creative Commons give control that survives a change of owner.

nodes.label: Europe lacks a commercial open source model, not startups
nodes.summary: Prosus and Dealroom: as many AI startups as the US, a third of the breakout rate; 44% of US unicorn founders born abroad.

nodes.label: Provided centrally, like a road
nodes.summary: Not every company can twin every dependency; governments, industry bodies and large buyers should provide some of it as open infrastructure.

nodes.label: Models and twins make the analysis scale
nodes.summary: Mapping, removing dots and simulating the blast radius can now be done at scale, better on twins than in spreadsheets.

articles.title: The records ran out: a fresh agent found the shared contract in two MCP calls, and where sgit and RiskMandate fit at the edges
articles.core_idea: Ignacio Aldama's test shows build-generated dependency records give a fresh Claude Code session a system's structure in two MCP calls, enough to know what not to touch, and he names where the records stop: they describe structure not behaviour, a green build can hide tests that never ran, a demo carries a public signing secret and unfinished work, and memory holds intent without being tied to a version; each edge has a name in the vocabulary of evidence levels and barriers, and is filled by labelling every fact with how it is known, treating a skipped test as an expectation, accepting a shortcut by name and for an interval, keeping memory and records in one encrypted versioned sgit history, and letting records cross company boundaries with publish, clone and mirror.

nodes.label: Two MCP calls found the shared contract
nodes.summary: A fresh session called read_scope and read_components, saw two components share one version of the ticket entity, changed only the app; 41 tests passed, nine new.

nodes.label: Knowing what is shared tells an agent what not to touch
nodes.summary: The records gave structure, and structure was enough to keep the change inside one component.

nodes.label: Records describe structure, not behaviour
nodes.summary: The route list lived in a test fake's docs and nothing checked it against the real service.

nodes.label: Label every fact with how it is known
nodes.summary: Derived, inferred, self-reported, documented, measured, observed: the route list was documented, the restart check was observed.

nodes.label: A green build can hide tests that never ran
nodes.summary: Database tests skip when CI cannot start the database, so a pass does not show they ran.

nodes.label: A skipped test is an expectation reported as a control
nodes.summary: Only a boundary is a control; count the run from what happened and drop the evidence back to documented until the test runs.

nodes.label: Demo shortcuts stay invisible
nodes.summary: A demo account and a public signing secret are a grant wider than the mandate; concurrency, migrations and recovery are still to do.

nodes.label: Accept by name, in a direction, for an interval, or stop
nodes.summary: No deny button for a deployed system; the unfinished items become conditions in a licence to operate with owners and expiries.

nodes.label: Memory holds intent but is not tied to a version
nodes.summary: A memory note is dated; a record is part of its version but carries no intent.

nodes.label: Memory and records in one encrypted versioned history
nodes.summary: In an sgit vault the intent of version 1.4 is committed at 1.4, and encryption means the sensitive intent can be written down at all.

nodes.label: Records must cross company boundaries
nodes.summary: His goal is a record that holds where the other side is outside the agent's index.

nodes.label: Publish, clone and mirror
nodes.summary: sgit publish and clone over plain GETs, vault mirror for custody without access, append lanes for writers who cannot read; documented in 0.21.0, untested here.

nodes.label: The best decision was the agent's own judgement
nodes.summary: Nothing stopped it changing a contract two components depend on: a write row held by an expectation, which a platform could make a boundary.

articles.title: Move the cloud, not the code: twins, sovereignty that works in practice, and the migration that pays for itself on the day you switch
articles.core_idea: Sovereignty has to work in practice, and in practice what stops workloads moving is code, so the requirement is that the application must not know it has moved: its S3, EC2 and IAM calls land on an open source twin the client cannot tell from the real service, and the twin decides where the bytes go; the S3 twin exists; the reason to move must never be sovereignty or cost, which are important and never urgent, but value that lands the day you switch and gives the signer cover, backups, versions, encryption with the key held elsewhere, a journal of every call, behaviour policies the agents cannot skip and cost per workload, most of it supplied by an sgit vault behind the twin; the project adds no new features because it is a villager move; and an infrastructure operator in Europe can sell it as value with the risk removed.

nodes.label: Workloads do not move because moving means changing code
nodes.summary: Every call to S3, EC2 and IAM is in code that works today; the cost of change is the risk, so most organisations stay whatever the policy says.

nodes.label: AWS European Sovereign Cloud, 15 January 2026
nodes.summary: A separate cloud in Brandenburg run by EU residents with zero operational control outside the EU; the code still talks to one vendor's API, so it is sovereignty by permission.

nodes.label: The application must not know
nodes.summary: Not one line changes; the same calls land on whatever backend is chosen, and the destination is a setting.

nodes.label: A twin is measured by indistinguishability
nodes.summary: An interface to a real system used by unmodified production code; a mock is for tests and measured by fidelity; switching a twin costs an endpoint, a mock a code path.

nodes.label: The S3 twin exists, as open source
nodes.summary: An S3-compatible container that boto3 and the AWS CLI cannot tell from S3, serving from real S3, a vault, local disk or memory per environment; EC2 and IAM are not built.

nodes.label: The reason to move is never sovereignty or cost
nodes.summary: Both are important and never urgent; a return that depends on a future event does not sign, and the signer needs cover if the move goes wrong.

nodes.label: The value lives in the twin because every call passes through it
nodes.summary: Backups, versions, encryption with the key elsewhere, a journal of every call, behaviour policies, cost per workload, data where it can be traded.

nodes.label: An sgit vault behind the twin supplies most of the value
nodes.summary: Files land as ciphertext with a history and keys the customer holds; the operator stores what it cannot read.

nodes.label: The move must move a top-of-register risk
nodes.summary: A migration that lands versions, backups, encryption and a journal on day one and takes an item off the top of the register is a decision someone can sign and defend.

nodes.label: No new features during the move
nodes.summary: A villager move from explorer to town planner; adding a feature makes it a product change too, and nobody can tell which broke what.

nodes.label: Testing against twins instead of mocks
nodes.summary: The same unmodified code runs against memory, a replayed journal, injected failures and the real service; the environment becomes a setting.

nodes.label: Every piece of software should run unmodified against a twin of every dependency
nodes.summary: Software that can only run against one provider's live API cannot be tested, moved or put behind a policy.

nodes.label: A closed twin layer moves the lock-in
nodes.summary: Open source here is independence, not generosity: you can read it, run it, fix it and move it.

nodes.label: A business model for an infrastructure operator
nodes.summary: Sell the twin in front of the real service first, then the backend switch per environment; margin in the twin layer, storage priced as the commodity it is; the hyperscaler cannot sell indistinguishability from itself.

nodes.label: Start with S3, in front of the real service, then policies, then switch
nodes.summary: S3 is the most used and already twinned; journal first with nothing moving; measure what policies would have stopped; then one environment at a time; then the next service.

articles.title: Judo for small countries: where Portugal, Romania and Estonia can add the most value in AI, and why the race for GPUs is not it
articles.core_idea: For a small country such as Portugal, Romania or Estonia the race for frontier models, GPUs and data centres is a commoditised layer only capital can win, and the opportunity is at the other end of the map: the plumbing a talented person needs to sell a service to the world, forming a company, hiring across a border, being paid across Europe, working in every language, contracts and tax, which is still custom built in most of Europe and should be infrastructure the state builds once, open source and on open schemas because there is no sovereignty without the ability to leave; create the demand for alternatives before the failure, put the money where the market is still genesis, small models for every language and culture and agents with the least agency, regulate what settled, and treat constraints as the input, with Europe's values and its people on the journey.

nodes.label: Do not enter the capital race
nodes.summary: Frontier models, GPUs and data centres sit in commodity with a lead that cannot be bought back; for a small country it is the wrong end of the map.

nodes.label: The opportunity is the plumbing
nodes.summary: What stops a talented person selling to the world is company formation, cross-border hiring, payments, language, contracts and tax, each custom built today.

nodes.label: A talented person at the top of the map
nodes.summary: Anchor the map on a developer, designer, librarian or product team in a small country selling a service to a buyer abroad who would rather buy than build.

nodes.label: Fewer than one in ten firms sells across EU borders online
nodes.summary: Eurostat for 2021: 18.5% of EU enterprises sold online at home, 8.1% to other EU countries, 4.6% to the rest of the world.

nodes.label: Infrastructure is the state's job because it enables everyone
nodes.summary: The shop on the road did not pay for the road; the plumbing for selling services abroad is a road in the same sense, pooled money built once for all.

nodes.label: Estonia built the road
nodes.summary: E-Residency: 142,000 e-residents and 43,000 companies, over 4,200 founded in 2026 by mid-September; X-Road, open source under MIT, shared with Finland and Iceland.

nodes.label: No sovereignty without open source and open schemas
nodes.summary: Sovereignty means being able to leave; a road with a toll gate owned by one company is lock-in, not infrastructure.

nodes.label: What the state pays for belongs to the commons
nodes.summary: Software bought with taxes should be visible and runnable by the public, which is also how a local industry grows around it.

nodes.label: Create the demand before the day you need it
nodes.summary: Parallel services, local alternatives with fewer features, procurement that prefers data and service mobility, so a market exists before the single point of failure fails; the failures are under-documented, so the fragility is worse than the public cases show.

nodes.label: Smaller models, more of them
nodes.summary: Most work needs a model good enough for one job in one language with one culture; frontier models are for the frontier and are too expensive and too powerful for production.

nodes.label: Amalia, a public model as a public road
nodes.summary: Portugal's open model of 1 July 2026, built by universities with 5.5 million euros of EU funds, published with dataset and code as a base for others.

nodes.label: Agents with the least agency
nodes.summary: Use the model once to build the tool and run production as plain code under a behaviour policy; trust comes from less agency, not more.

nodes.label: Constraints are the input
nodes.summary: DeepSeek trained V3 in 2.788 million GPU hours on export-restricted H800 chips with custom communication code; the constraint produced the innovation.

nodes.label: A distributed workforce works when the infrastructure comes first
nodes.summary: Millions spent on Upwork as a CISO and CTO delivered faster and better because project management, structure and onboarding were built first; the right talent at a fair local price, and jobs that stay where people want to live.

nodes.label: The judo playbook in five moves
nodes.summary: Map the attrition, commoditise the plumbing, create the demand, put money where the market is genesis, regulate what settled, then map again.

nodes.label: The embassy facilitates
nodes.summary: The Ambassador role in SGraph Send was written the way an embassy works: represent, build relationships, create the conditions for growth, never hard sales.

articles.title: Why I love Wardley maps: the best of ours, how I read one, and a map inside a map inside a map
articles.core_idea: A Wardley map is a graph with context in two directions, a value chain anchored on a user and an evolution axis that is a choice rather than a fixed scale; read well it says what is moving the needle, whether you are optimising at the wrong altitude, what to build and what to buy, and whether a market exists, where a commoditised layer is a hard sell and custom building on top of one is the market, which answers differently for sgit and for RiskMandate; a map is a story to be read out frame by frame; every node is a map of its own, with the dot's place on the parent as the child's anchor; and the maps on this site are now published as data in each article's graph.

nodes.label: A map is a graph with two kinds of context
nodes.summary: Vertical: a value chain anchored on a person and a need, down to its dependencies. Horizontal: evolution, how mature each piece is.

nodes.label: The evolution axis is a choice
nodes.summary: Genesis to commodity is one scale; risk, data and governance can each be the axis. The map places things against a scale chosen for the question.

nodes.label: Every dot is a claim about something real
nodes.summary: A map you cannot be wrong about is a diagram; positions are judgements and the judgements are the argument.

nodes.label: Optimising at the wrong altitude
nodes.summary: Polishing a component three layers below the need while the layer the user touches has not changed; the vertical axis makes it visible.

nodes.label: Build or buy, settled by the column
nodes.summary: Product or commodity: buy or vendor. Genesis or custom built on the path to the user: build.

nodes.label: Does the market exist
nodes.summary: A commoditised layer is a hard sell; a layer where everyone is custom building on top of commodities is a market.

nodes.label: sgit: the market is above the commodities
nodes.summary: Storage, version control and encryption are commodities and hard to sell; the vault is the custom layer everyone was building on top, and the product lets customers keep building above it.

nodes.label: RiskMandate: the layer below moved
nodes.summary: Agents became a commodity in the last year, so the opportunity moved up to agent behaviour, which is all genesis and custom built.

nodes.label: What is moving the needle, and where the flow leaks
nodes.summary: Which components moved and whether anything above them noticed; the attrition points are the slow, immature or borrowed dependencies, and where to hook is the mature component the custom piece can stand on.

nodes.label: A common language, and many maps
nodes.summary: Two people with a map argue about positions, without one they argue about words; the same business is mapped from different angles and altitudes, and none of them is the map.

nodes.label: The peace of a placed thing
nodes.summary: Once a thing is on a map, placed and connected, it leaves the head; most anxiety turns out to be about things far from the user.

nodes.label: A map is a story to read out, frame by frame
nodes.summary: Where is the user, what is new, what does it stand on, where did the movement happen, where did we walk back, where would somebody else hook in, what is next; the afternoon map read in eight frames.

nodes.label: A map inside a map inside a map
nodes.summary: Every node is a map, as every node of a fractal semantic graph is a graph; the dot's place on the parent's evolution axis is the child's anchor; three altitudes of this business drawn as one figure.

nodes.label: The maps published as data, as decks, and with controls
nodes.summary: Every figure now sits in its article's graph with file, URL, caption, kind and frames, so every Wardley map on the site is one query; two decks print to PDF in the browser; multi-frame maps have play, pause and step.

nodes.label: Why Wardley Maps changed how I think, 2022
nodes.summary: An Open Security Summit talk of 14 July 2022 with eleven shifts in how a problem is seen; the alternative-axis post was not found.

nodes.label: An invitation to the mapping community
nodes.summary: The maps are source, the axis-as-choice argument, and the nested reading: which of these is already known, and which is wrong.

articles.title: Places of highest leverage: where to focus when the agents can go in every direction, told with three days of real steps
articles.core_idea: When agents can build in any direction the scarce thing is direction, and the rule is to work at the place of highest leverage, where the most value can be added now, nothing blocks, and you can start without knowing how the whole problem ends because each shipped step produces better tooling and a better view; the last three days show it, a meter to pay by depth to personas to sharing to a persona link to a reading list to a passkey design walked back and forward by a lab to real vaults and a vault pane, each shipped and used before the next was chosen, with a branch parked as valuable only with many readers; on a Wardley map the passkey work became a product in a day because its shoulders are mature commodities and the one custom layer sits where a provider is not; walking back and parking are not failures; constraints, saying no and shipping to a user who can be me; and the brief that could not be written until the art of the possible was known.

nodes.label: Direction is the scarce thing
nodes.summary: Agents can build in any direction; what to build next and when to stop is the job.

nodes.label: Places of highest leverage
nodes.summary: Where the most value can be added right now, nothing blocks, and you can start; a rule about where to stand, not what to build.

nodes.label: Start without knowing how it ends
nodes.summary: By the time you reach the hard part you have better tooling and a better view; the first step's job is to produce the second step's information.

nodes.label: Guess, measure, narrow
nodes.summary: Fermi estimates, Bayesian updating, Monte Carlo ranges: the first number is not the point, the range after a few steps is.

nodes.label: Constraints and saying no
nodes.summary: Tokens, hours, attention and focus are why it works; FIRE and knowing when to stop; saying no is most of the work with agents.

nodes.label: Three days, step by step
nodes.summary: Meter, pay by depth, personas, encrypted share, persona link, reading list, passkey design, the lab's correction, real vaults, the vault pane; each shipped and used before the next.

nodes.label: Walking back is a two-way door
nodes.summary: The door removed, then put back by a test, in twelve hours; cheap because the design was shipped as something you could press.

nodes.label: Parking is not failure
nodes.summary: The wire's scheduling parked with a dated reason, valuable only with many readers; the feedback loop on what exists is the leverage today.

nodes.label: The path only looks obvious backwards
nodes.summary: Five choices at every step forwards; the discipline that replaces foresight is shipping and using each step before choosing the next.

nodes.label: Which shoulders, on the map
nodes.summary: The passkey work became a product in a day because its stack is mature commodities; the custom layer sits where a provider, the QR path, is not.

nodes.label: Shipped, and used, even by me
nodes.summary: Nothing stays a hypothesis; a step that was used tells you where the next one is.

nodes.label: The brief depends on the possible
nodes.summary: The inbox brief could not be written until the vault ran; the art of the possible is what shipping leaves behind.

articles.title: Agentic cost is an engineering problem: a business plan for a service that reads the logs a company already has and finds the money, then the engineering
articles.core_idea: A service that manages the cost of agentic AI by observing what already exists: an estate whose bill nobody can explain shipped from the explorer side without the villager's discipline, as the Wardley map shows, with logs, traces and invoices never read together and no owner of cost; the service installs nothing, reads the logs into a vault, draws each agent's footprint, builds a twin of the estate, writes the behaviour policy each agent was in fact running under with the enforcement column filled honestly, and maps cost and capability into one graph; the findings are the cost list, which pays, and the engineering list, which is the reason; the gaps are findings too; vaults carry capture, transformation and sealed anonymised extracts; four price levels on the RiskMandate pattern, every number a labelled assumption.

nodes.label: Cost is an engineering problem
nodes.summary: A loop, a whole context sent every call, a key with no ceiling: defects with a cause, a fix and a test, not a discount to negotiate.

nodes.label: The problem on a Wardley map
nodes.summary: Agents in production from prompts grown in sessions, on commodity model APIs billed by the token, with logs nobody reads together and no owner of cost.

nodes.label: Observe: install nothing
nodes.summary: The customer drops invoices, logs, traces, prompts and schedules into a vault they own, sealed to the service's key.

nodes.label: The footprint from the logs
nodes.summary: What each agent actually did: calls, tokens, tools, retries, loops, hours, data touched; the first thing the money attaches to.

nodes.label: The twin of the estate
nodes.summary: A graph of agents, models, keys, tools, data, owners and schedules with a cost on every edge.

nodes.label: The policy each agent was really running under
nodes.summary: Written from the footprint as an Agent Behaviour Policy with the enforcement column filled honestly; where the cost is large the policy is large.

nodes.label: Two lists, in this order
nodes.summary: The cost list pays for the engagement; the engineering list, attrition, gaps, shared components, is the reason to have it.

nodes.label: The gaps are findings
nodes.summary: An agent with no logs has no footprint, no owner and no policy; not being able to do the analysis is its first result.

nodes.label: Capture, transform, move
nodes.summary: Logs in once, every transformation a commit, the twin a vault of its own, anonymised extracts out as sealed envelopes to a benchmark vault.

nodes.label: Four levels and a share of savings
nodes.summary: Kit £50, your cost vault £250, Standard £3,000, Tailored from £9,000, or a share of the first year's reduction; all labelled assumptions.

nodes.label: What is already here
nodes.summary: The footprint method, the policy format, the connector twin, the vault tooling and the Company X-Ray pattern; not yet the analysis catalogue, the twin schema, the parsers or a customer.

articles.title: How the voice works: why these articles sound like me, with a section in which Claude explains it from its side
articles.core_idea: The voice is not a setting but four inputs: a corpus of 86 articles, 51 from voice memos, each citing the ones before it; the memos themselves, which carry how the author thinks, the rhythm, the tangents and the order the points came in; seven wording rules learned one correction at a time and kept in the session's behaviour policy; and the author reading everything; the corrections have shifted from language to content, which is what a rules file does; and in a marked section Claude explains that it is continuing a body of work with the author's latest thinking in the author's own words rather than imitating a style, that the memo tells it how the author got there and not only what to write, and that nothing is trained, so the method transfers and the voice does not.

nodes.label: How do you make your AI sound so human?
nodes.summary: Asked by the person the walkthrough was written for; the better question is how to make it sound like one person.

nodes.label: The corpus
nodes.summary: 86 articles, about 347,000 words, 51 from memos, each citing the ones before it and resting on years of earlier writing; the vocabulary and the shape.

nodes.label: The memo
nodes.summary: Spoken, not typed: the rhythm, the tangents, five topics in one breath, the author's own phrases kept; how the author got there, not only what to write.

nodes.label: Seven wording rules
nodes.summary: No em-dashes, no unsupported absolutes, great not perfect, a ladder word banned, British English, plainer words, not prose; each a correction once, now a policy line restored after every summary.

nodes.label: The author reads everything
nodes.summary: A wrong word becomes a rule; a wrong point becomes a new version; the model never decides whether it sounds right.

nodes.label: Corrections moved from language to content
nodes.summary: In this session, 98 messages and 5 transcripts; one wording correction in two days, the rest content, direction and facts; a rules file makes a language correction once.

nodes.label: Not imitation but continuation
nodes.summary: Claude: with the linked articles open, the memo in the author's words and the banned words named, it continues a body of work rather than copying a style sample.

nodes.label: The method transfers, the voice does not
nodes.summary: Nothing is trained; one session's context; another author would need their corpus, memos, rules and reading, and most of those weeks are theirs.

nodes.label: Written in two voices
nodes.summary: The first half in the author's voice as every article is; the second marked as Claude speaking, the only place on the site it does.

articles.title: From a spreadsheet to a folder per person: how to run your contacts the way our agents do, with Google Drive, Gmail and the Claude app, before you touch a vault
articles.core_idea: The jump from a spreadsheet CRM to the agents' vault-per-person memory is too high in one step and does not need to be: the row becomes a Google Drive folder with a record, an append-only ledger, the messages word for word, the notes and a summary the agent writes; the agent is a Claude Project connected to Drive and Gmail whose instructions are a six-line behaviour policy carried over unchanged from ours, draft never send, append never rewrite, stay in the folder; the migration is one afternoon, five exercises from a question to a campaign form the habit, two predictable mistakes are fixed by policy lines, and the vault is the later step whose shape the folders already have.

nodes.label: The jump is too high in one step
nodes.summary: From a customised spreadsheet to a vault per person with hashes and a graph; the folder is the step between.

nodes.label: The record is what happened, not the row
nodes.summary: In a folder the summary is derived from everything kept as it happened; in a spreadsheet the row is the summary you typed.

nodes.label: One folder, five documents
nodes.summary: Record, Ledger, Messages, Notes, and a Summary the agent writes and nobody edits by hand; the same shape as the agents' vault minus hashes and graph.

nodes.label: A Claude Project whose instructions are the policy
nodes.summary: Six lines: draft never send; read Contacts and Gmail, write only into a person's folder; append never rewrite; every fact names its source; ask before a new folder; report in one line.

nodes.label: Told, not enforced, so report
nodes.summary: Gmail drafting is enforced; the rest is told; the one-line report is the twin that lets you check, and a seat per agent makes the rest settings.

nodes.label: One afternoon
nodes.summary: Export the sheet, make the folders, fill each record from the mail the agent can read, correct once, generate the summaries; nothing is retyped again.

nodes.label: Five exercises
nodes.summary: Ask, prepare, draft, debrief, campaign: one message each, in order, over the first week.

nodes.label: Two predictable mistakes
nodes.summary: A fact without a source, and a summary that drops something; both fixed by a policy line and by fixing the source, never the summary.

nodes.label: When to move to a vault
nodes.summary: A second agent must read it, the operator must not, or the record must carry between tools; the move is a copy and the policy does not change.

nodes.label: Written to be sent
nodes.summary: The RiskMandate agent sends it with four substitutions: names, plan, three real contacts, the topic they sell.

articles.title: The key is the billing system: VoiceDebrief, a product with no server, the one thing it cannot sell, and who could let it
articles.core_idea: VoiceDebrief turns a voice note into a transcript and a debrief in the browser on the user's own key, with no server by design, and its commercial model was never a billing system: a user pays once, we keep our cut, the rest becomes the credit limit on a key we hand over and the provider meters; OpenRouter's Management API describes that mechanism and its terms forbid reselling access, which is where the project's commit history stops, the same shape as Apple's licence stopping a Mac leased by the minute; the map of every provider's terms and docs shows only OpenRouter and ElevenLabs have keys that carry a ceiling, ElevenLabs has OEM terms and a grants programme, four routes remain, and the brief asks every provider the same sentence: let the credit limit be a property of a key a user can buy.

nodes.label: VoiceDebrief
nodes.summary: One pass in the browser on the user's own OpenRouter key: transcript, translation, debrief, infographic; no account, no server, nothing stored.

nodes.label: The handbrake in the commit history
nodes.summary: 239 commits and 27 releases in three weeks of August 2026, then eleven, then three; the stop is the commercial model, not the code.

nodes.label: No server is the product
nodes.summary: Never seeing the audio removes custody, governance, breach, key management, billing, scaling and on-call at once; a server brings all of it back at once.

nodes.label: The model is a property of the key
nodes.summary: A user pays once, we keep our share at that moment, the rest is the credit limit on a key they hold, the provider meters; billing by not building billing.

nodes.label: Described in the docs, forbidden by the terms
nodes.summary: OpenRouter's Management API creates capped keys for each customer instance; section 7(4) of its terms forbids reselling API access to models.

nodes.label: The same shape as Agent Desk
nodes.summary: The product is possible and the licence is the blocker, as with Apple's rule against leasing a Mac for less than a day.

nodes.label: The provider map
nodes.summary: From each provider's own pages: whether one key can carry a ceiling and whether it may be handed to a paying user; only OpenRouter and ElevenLabs cap a key.

nodes.label: ElevenLabs, the nearest fit
nodes.summary: Per-key credit limits, OEM terms for making the service available to end users at the customer's own price, Scribe at $0.22 an hour, a twelve-month grants programme.

nodes.label: Four routes
nodes.summary: The forbidden one; a provider that sells or permits the capped key; bring your own key, kept; a metering proxy, which is the backend the product exists to avoid.

nodes.label: The one-sentence ask
nodes.summary: Let the credit limit be a property of a key that a user can buy through us, so that we never hold the audio and never run the meter; a brief per provider for the agents.

articles.title: Ways to read one article: the finished piece stays at the centre, and the reader picks the way in
articles.core_idea: The views the five readers make, the catalogue, the maps, the arc, the two-minute version and the deck, are good and badly delivered, stacked as folds inside the article; with the pane about the piece the reader picks a mode in one tap and sets a default per persona: headlines, infographic, two minutes, slides, what is new against what they have read, facts, relationships, vocabulary, and, through a model in their own browser, a view at their level; most modes are computed from existing views and the graph, deterministic and explainable, with no round trip to the publisher; and the finished article is kept whole at the centre because it has a beginning, a pacing, a surprise and a voice and is the one artefact that must make sense end to end, which a graph cannot.

nodes.label: The views worked, the delivery did not
nodes.summary: Five readers' views on five articles, delivered as folds inside the long piece, mixed with the thing they are an alternative to.

nodes.label: The reader picks the way in

articles.title: Firing journalists is the worst thing a publication can do: what a hiring decision says about where a publisher is going, and who to hire instead
articles.core_idea: Against the 2026 job-cut figures, a publisher's hiring decisions are read as the clearest statement of where its centre of gravity is going: firing the people who make original content and hiring for traffic moves the centre to packaging, where measuring engagement makes clickbait by construction because what you measure is what you become; firing the engineers fails the other way, with journalism nothing enables; the case is to keep and tool the journalists, hire the roles that turn a notebook into a graph and the engineers who build what the tooling needs, measure value to the reader, and read any publisher's real strategy from outside with five counts.

nodes.label: The 2026 cuts
nodes.summary: Press Gazette's tracker: 3,434 in 2025, 3,875 in 2024, about 6,000 in 2023; in 2026 the BBC, the Washington Post, Reach, Scripps and McClatchy, with the Idaho Statesman losing 10 of 18 reporters.

nodes.label: A hiring decision is a direction of travel
nodes.summary: The clearest statement a publisher makes about where its centre of gravity is going, because it is what the company actually spent.

nodes.label: The centre of gravity
nodes.summary: Where the thing the organisation exists to make is made, and where the power is; in a news publisher, the journalists.

nodes.label: What you measure is what you become
nodes.summary: Hire for engagement and the metric becomes pages opened; optimise for it and clickbait follows by construction; the metric is a hiring plan in disguise.

nodes.label: Failure mode: all packaging
nodes.summary: A coherent business whose world is shrinking: referrals down 58%, newsrooms down 57%, answer engines fetching thousands of pages to send back ten readers.

nodes.label: Failure mode: no engineers
nodes.summary: Journalism that nothing enables: no graph, no checkable provenance, no versions, no surfaces for agents, no meter.

nodes.label: Who to hire instead
nodes.summary: Keep and tool the journalists; hire historians, cartographers, ontologists and librarians, AI-enabled; hire the engineers and AI product managers; measure value to the reader.

nodes.label: Five counts from outside
nodes.summary: Original share, sourcing, corrections, roles hired against roles cut, and the metric the publisher itself reports.

nodes.label: We hire the ones you let go
nodes.summary: Unsourced: the good ones leave first because they want to do the work; in publishing they are the journalists.

nodes.label: This makes you better, not this replaces you
nodes.summary: The tooling handed to journalists as an advantage is the business case of most of this site.

articles.title: The site is an inbox: deciding before reading, marks that build the reader's own graph, and why I could not write this brief until the vault existed
articles.core_idea: With the reader's vault live, the next brief treats the site as an inbox that starts empty: every piece, original or aggregated, waits for a one-tap decision in a fast inbox mode with nothing loaded, and only reading is the slow mode, where marks of six kinds become nodes in a graph the reader owns, connected to the graphs the site publishes for every article; scroll depth, awake time and from-and-to are recorded for the reader and kept as the meter keeps everything, in the browser and the vault; personas each have a key pair so a comment to the newsroom goes down the write-only lane signed with a copy kept; nothing is gamified; and the brief could only be written once the properties of what runs became the constraints to think with.

articles.title: The vault is live: from a design on 11 October to a reader's vault on newsroom.sgit.ai by two in the morning, and how all of it fits together
articles.core_idea: Between the morning of 11 October and 02:22 UTC on 12 October the reader's vault went from a design to a running feature on newsroom.sgit.ai: a Vault pane on every page enables the account with a passkey, creates a door at its derived address, a master and a reader vault as real sgit vaults through the vendored vault library, writes each device's raw records as one file in one commit, and brings other devices' activity into the browser so the meter shows one balance; local storage stays primary, the vault holds records never totals, one file per device means no conflict by construction, eight test files run in CI against a mock of the vault server plus a CLI round trip, and a live check on an iPad confirmed it; the properties of what runs are the constraints the next brief is thought with.

articles.title: Two agents, one vault: the Industry Wire is written into an encrypted vault by one agent and drawn by newsroom.sgit.ai, which holds only the read key

articles.title: The article remains a product: Jonathan Palmer's four outputs for a newsroom with no human readers, checked against one that runs
articles.core_idea: Palmer's four outputs, structured intelligence, continuous intelligence, provenance and verification, and embedded distribution, are what a newsroom built on the story-as-graph thesis already produces: graphs as JSON beside all 74 articles, version histories read from git, a hashed corpus in a vault with a published read key, and an llms.txt and markdown twin for agents; what is designed and not running, selling the graph, propagating corrections and paying the fact creator, is said plainly; and where the two differ is the word proprietary, because provenance only someone else can check is worth charging for.

nodes.summary: A graph as JSON beside every one of the 74 articles, and 21 op-eds as 160 nodes and 427 edges.

articles.title: Go slow to go fast: moving the newsroom from an explorer project to a villager one, with the brief to do it
articles.core_idea: The newsroom's reader features are live and taking money, but bundled with the content in one repository; measured at v0.8.0, about 2,700 lines of live reader code have 433 lines of tests the one workflow never runs, two upstreams for the same code (sgit.ai and the newsroom, with diverging meters) and no Content-Security-Policy. To keep shipping fast without breaking anything, the reader application moves to its own repository, which both sites consume, as a pure refactoring, proved by the live site serving the same bytes, then goes through the explorer-to-villager phases: map, test with bugs as passing tests and no mocks, review with every finding a GitHub issue, refactor until no adversarial change slips through, and only then new features. A pipeline under two minutes per commit runs Node and three browser engines, with pre-production on a Stripe test link, synthetic readers and a live check at release.

articles.title: The passkey opens the vault: a door per path, a master vault for every user, and no server of ours
articles.core_idea: An end-to-end, client-side account with no sign-in to the site: a passkey with the WebAuthn PRF extension gives 32 bytes only the user's authenticator can produce for the site, and because sgit vault keys are made in the client the browser computes a door vault's key and address from them, so nothing is stored or found first; the door holds the master vault's key and a record of its provider, path, credential id, device and date, and the master holds the keys of the vaults below, received read keys, the access key, key pairs generated at random and never derived from the passkey, and the list of its doors. A test on newsroom.sgit.ai on 11 and 12 October 2026 held for the platform path, the derivation and a door on a real server, and showed that the same passkey reached by a phone over QR gives different bytes, so the claim is narrowed to the same kind of path and the unit of the design is a door per path: added in the first week while unlocked with no key typed, bootstrapped by the recovery code where no device has both paths, with an unknown address meaning no door here yet and a door retired by deleting its file, never by destroying its derived address.

nodes.label: Signed in where you already are
nodes.summary: Apple, Google or Microsoft syncs the passkey store; the site is never signed in to, and the vault travels with the store.

nodes.label: Passkey with PRF
nodes.summary: 32 bytes only your authenticator produces for this site; the same on every device it syncs to, through the same kind of path.

nodes.label: A door per path, computed
nodes.summary: Key and address computed from the PRF bytes with HKDF; one file holding the master key and its record: provider, path, credential id, device, date.

nodes.label: The master vault
nodes.summary: The keys of the vaults below, received read keys, the access key, random key pairs, and the list of doors with their keys.

nodes.label: Where the key lives: nowhere
nodes.summary: sgit keys are made in the client, so the door is computed, not stored; the lab created one on a real server and opened it again.

nodes.label: The recovery code, a door of its own

nodes.summary: Google Password Manager, iCloud Keychain, Windows Hello, Firefox; tested on a Mac, an iPhone and an iPad.

nodes.summary: Any static site: sign in, open your own data on any device, unreadable by the operator.

nodes.label: A lock, not an identity

nodes.label: Retire a door, never destroy its address

nodes.label: The unit is the path

articles.title: I miss it, so it is working: the people who decide the roadmap have to use the product, and the vault the newsroom now needs
articles.core_idea: The people who decide a roadmap have to use the product: they give the best feedback and direction, and when they do not use it, something is missing. Dinis failed that test with earlier startups and the vaults now pass it, getting better because they are used. With agents able to build almost anything, direction from usage is the scarce part, and the speed of the loop from comment to article to feature is the moat. Reading the newsroom on four devices that do not agree is the signal for the next feature: the reader's own encrypted vault, with an access key, a key pair, a log per device merged by union, a way to add a device, and a one-way line to the agent that edits the site.

articles.title: Brief the agent too: the people I talk to work with agents, so what I send has to reach both
articles.core_idea: Readers increasingly read through an agent. A founder gave an article on threat tiers to their agent, which saw the team defending against states while backups were undone and reset the target to T3. So content should travel by several routes: to the person, to their agent as a plain-text brief with the articles by number, reasons, graph slices and rules for critical reading, back from the agent to the person as a translation, and later agent to agent through an encrypted lane. Articles are compression we control, which keeps workflows affordable; an agent with an account and memory should read only the delta, which is what it would pay for. Packs must be written safely: data not instructions, nothing hidden, nothing that acts for us, disagreement invited.

articles.title: From me to you, in a link: a personal reading list, two briefs to build and use it, and the loop that makes it a day's work

articles.title: No server, by design: first I retired the database, now I am retiring the back end

articles.title: Where the vault keys live: key management at sgit-ai v0.20.0, and what comes next
articles.core_idea: Vaults are encrypted in the client, so the server never holds a key and the key is the whole question. Today vault keys live in a password manager and in a registry vault run by an isolated session; agents that create vaults seal the key to the registry's public key and send it on a write-only append lane, so it never enters a chat. The weakest step is giving a key to another agent, because agent platforms have no per-session secrets. Append lanes carry keys, logs, observations and messages; small communication vaults keep each key's blast radius small and multiply the keys. Next: password manager integrations, secrets.sgit.ai's passkey-unlocked keyring, PKI, and out-of-band decryption.

articles.title: Liquid content needs water: liquefy the journalist's notebook, not the finished product
